\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:7}\ThesisCheckNumber{section}{7}

This thesis examined the association between water and sanitation conditions and the anthropometric outcomes of children in four Sub-Saharan African countries: Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya and Nigeria. Two distinctions ran through the analysis. The first is between a child's own household facilities and the WASH conditions of the surrounding community. The second is between a single exposure measured at the survey date and a preliminary, geospatially matched measure of modelled local WASH coverage during the child's own early-life window. The second measure was constructed for an earlier survey round in three of the four countries, with Ethiopia retained only as a provisional sensitivity analysis (Section~1.4).

The baseline evidence does not show a clear, robust association between improved household WASH and child height-for-age, weight-for-age or weight-for-height when households are compared within the same DHS cluster. None of the six household cluster-fixed-effects coefficients (three outcomes, two exposures) reaches significance at the 5\% level under this thesis's primary inference convention; household water--HAZ, with \emph{p} = .062, crosses only a 10\% threshold (Section~5.1). Under this design, that is an inconclusive result, not evidence that no association exists.

The community measure answers a related but distinct question. It is a leave-one-out coverage rate among the other sampled households in the cluster, and it is estimated with region rather than cluster fixed effects (Sections~4.3 and 5.2). Community coverage shows a large, strongly significant association before adjustment for most outcome and exposure pairs. Weight-for-height water is the exception: it is small and non-significant from the start. Once socioeconomic status and region fixed effects are added, the association is no longer statistically significant for any pair. This attenuation is consistent with confounding by local development, but the design cannot establish confounding as the only explanation.

These baseline findings are broadly consistent with the strongest available causal evidence on WASH interventions. In the three major trials, the basic, household-level WASH interventions tested showed no statistically detectable effect on linear growth, and the trial authors state explicitly that this does not challenge the biological plausibility of WASH affecting growth \autocite{Cumming2019}. The parallel is suggestive rather than confirmatory, because the exposure in this thesis is a facility-type classification in survey data, not a randomised, comprehensive intervention package (Section~2.3).

The historical extension links earlier DHS rounds from Ghana, Kenya and Nigeria to IHME's modelled annual local WASH coverage for a defined early-life window. Its exposure is an area average of modelled coverage around displaced cluster coordinates; it is neither observed historical household access nor population-weighted coverage (Sections~3.5 and 6.5). The selected headline cell is the pooled established-date association between local water coverage and height-for-age: β = 1.03 per 10 percentage points (95\% CI {[}0.51, 1.54{]}, \emph{p} \textless{} .001). It is not the only nominally significant historical result. Six of the 24 primary cells have \emph{p} \textless{} .05, one of them a negative Ghana sanitation cell (Section~5.6). The headline cell was reconstructed independently with a second estimation library on a separately rebuilt sample, as were all 24 primary cells; the other 267 of the 291 historical models passed internal checks but, apart from two unweighted counterparts, were not re-estimated in this way (Appendix~B). This reproduction confirms the computation. It does not adjust for the number of cells tested, and it does not make the association causal.

The headline finding carries the qualifications set out in Section~6. It depends on the pooled weighting convention: on the same 23,018 observations, the unweighted estimate is β = 0.41 (95\% CI {[}0.03, 0.80{]}, \emph{p} = .035), and equal country weight totals do not give the three countries equal influence on the pooled slope (Section~5.6). The weighting of the measured subsample relies on a working inference, because no official documentation of an anthropometry-specific sampling weight could be located (Section~6.3). The estimates are therefore weighted conditional associations among eligible measured children, not population-representative effects. The exposure source draws on the DHS surveys of Ghana and Kenya themselves, current residence stands in for early-life residence, and the residual within-cluster exposure variation that identifies the model is much smaller than the 10-point reporting scale (Section~6.5). Ethiopia's estimates remain provisional and outside the established-date pooled family. Finally, the contrast with the baseline results cannot be attributed to exposure timing, because the two samples differ at the same time in their children and survey rounds, exposure construction, eligibility rules and control sets (Section~6.2). The historical result is a preliminary, qualified finding rather than a settled one, and this thesis does not use it to overturn or reinterpret the more cautious baseline conclusions.

Taken together, the thesis makes two separate contributions in two separate samples (Section~1.5). In the baseline sample, it compares own-household and leave-one-out community WASH exposure side by side, within one four-country sample and one consistent set of controls, with each exposure estimated under the fixed-effects structure its construction requires. In the historical sample, it makes a documented, preliminary attempt to introduce genuine temporal variation in early-life exposure through geospatially matched coverage data. Because the historical data cannot separate a child's own household from its community, this second contribution does not extend the household-versus-community comparison.

Neither set of results, alone or together, establishes a causal effect of WASH facilities on child nutritional outcomes in these four countries. Fixed effects remove only what is shared within a region or cluster, and the four countries were selected for data availability and recency, not to represent Sub-Saharan Africa as a whole (Sections~1.4 and 6.6). Nor can the results be read as evidence for or against the value of WASH investment as a development policy. Weak or inconclusive nutritional associations in an associational, four-country design do not show that such investment lacks value, and no causal policy effect or cost-effectiveness was estimated. What the thesis offers instead is an account of where its evidence is stronger, where it is weaker, and where further data or a different design would be needed before a stronger claim could responsibly be made. The two clearest gaps are the unresolved measurement documentation of the historical extension and the exposure-timing limitation inherent in the baseline design.

Future work could address these gaps in three ways that follow directly from the limitations above. First, validating the Ethiopian interview-date conversion would allow the historical approach to cover all four countries on an established-date basis (Appendix~C). Second, the measurement-subsample weighting question could be resolved through direct engagement with DHS methodological documentation. Third, geospatial WASH matching could be combined with a design that follows the same geographic units over successive survey rounds (Section~1.2). These would be natural next steps toward narrowing the gap that this thesis has described but not closed.
